newsitem.title: USA: U.S. REFINERS MULL IRAQI CRUDES, BRENT PRICE EASES.
newsitem.headline: U.S. REFINERS MULL IRAQI CRUDES, BRENT PRICE EASES.

text.p: U.S. refiners began to mull preliminary offers for Iraqi crude oil on Wednesday in anticipation of renewed humanitarian exports, traders said.
Two sellers were heard offering late September cargoes of Basrah Light and Kirkuk crude.
Basrah was pegged around $2.00-2.05 a barrel under West Texas Intermediate/Cushing, while Kirkuk was offered around $1.90-2.00 under the benchmark, traders said.

While several spot cargoes of Basrah found homes in the U.S. Gulf during the first six months of Iraq's "oil-for-food deal," traders said this would be the first time that Kirkuk made its way into the Atlantic Basin since before Iraq invaded Kuwait in 1990.
One Gulf trader explained that Kirkuk's formula has been shifted in this round of sales from second-line WTI to front-line WTI, improving the economics of delivery.
Elsewhere in U.S. foreign crude trade, the delivered price for North Sea Brent softened on Wednesday, reflecting the weaker Dated Brent price in Europe.
The benchmark grade was priced around 35 cents under October WTI for late September arrival in the U.S. Gulf, although interest was seen as tepid amid plentiful alternative supply.
Several sweet West African cargoes, as well as Colombian Cusiana shipments, were looking for homes.
A European company was showing Nigerian Bonny Light for September 10-15, asking Dated Brent plus $1.69 a barrel, not including lightering costs of around 30 cents.
Several Qua Iboe cargoes were also outstanding at around $1.90 over Dated Brent.
Reflecting recent price volatility, Cusiana cargoes were on offer at 60-78 cents under October WTI for mid-September delivery.
Four cargoes of the September program have been sold, with the latest sale from Colombian state oil company Ecopetrol to a U.S. refiner for September 14-18 loading.
A U.S. company resold its September 5-9 Cusiana at an undisclosed price earlier this week, while two other buyers were also attempting to resell.
The efforts to resell the popular grade reflect firming freight rates in the Caribbean and the drop in Dated Brent, traders said.
"Cusiana doesn't look as good as it did a few days ago," a U.S. trader said.
